title: 'We've been looking for 47 years:' North Alabama woman ramps up search for former foster child - NewsBreak
text:
By Lauren Layton ,
1 hours ago
MADISON COUNTY, Ala. ( WHNT ) — For some, a life’s wish is extravagant, but for Terry Nayman, it is simply to know that a former foster child of hers is happy.
Goo Goo Dolls to perform at The Wharf “When she smiled, her eyes smiled,” Nayman said as she looked at a portrait. It is the only photograph she has of Kami. She was four months old at the time of the picture. She’s kept it for 47 years now.
“She was born in Huntsville Hospital on August the 10th, 1978” Naman said. “She came to live with us when she was four days old.”
Her daughters, Robyn Brumlow and Stephanie McDaniel, were six and 12 years old at the time.
“She was a part of our family,” McDaniel said.
“We named her when she came home from the hospital,” Brumlow added.
For them, family is not defined by blood. The Naymans fostered children for 15 years.
“There’s still a need today, but at that time, it was a great need,” Nayman said. “It was in the papers asking people to be foster parents.”
With the girls in school and Nayman at home, she said having more children to care for was a call she had to answer.
“When they would tell you about things that they had gone through, it was hard to accept those things, you know, and you wanted to fix them,” she said. “You have to pour your heart out and really love them, and it’s not hard to love them.”
The whole family agreed that all they wanted was to offer those children a safe place and a sense of family.
Kami was their first foster child.
“In fact, we tried to adopt, but, according to DHR, we were not eligible,” Nayman said.
After nearly a year in the family’s care, Kami was moved.
“We were told she went to South Alabama and was adopted by a couple. They had a son, who was also adopted. The name they gave us, [for Kami], was ‘Heather Elizabeth.’
To this day, she said Kami was their hardest goodbye.
“It was hard to give up a child that you had taken as an infant, four days old, and then give up at ten months old. She was ours,” Nayman said.
McDaniel remembers that day well.
“It was pure grief, because she had become our sister,” she said.
Terry explained that since the time she left, they’ve always wondered how she was doing. They tried finding her on the internet once she turned 18, but without more information, all searches came up short.
Recently, though, Nayman ramped up the search again.
“I was diagnosed with cancer. It’s in remission now, thank God, but that made me more anxious to see her. I just don’t know how much time I have left,” Nayman said.
This month, she had the idea to take all of the information she had and publish it to Facebook , on the page for lost family members around the U.S. She also published it locally.
People all over the state were moved by her story. Within the first day, there were nearly 1,500 shares.
“It’s just so overwhelming to see all these people. So many people out there that want us to find her!”
She said the comments were the most heartwarming part.
“Some of them are foster parents, some of them are adoptees, and they are all trying.”
Her daughters say as much as they want to hug Kami, or Heather Elizabeth, again, they want to reunite most with their parents.
“It would be the best Christmas present in the world for mom, mom, and dad to be able to see her again,” McDaniel said.
Kami, or Heather Elizabeth, was born August 10, 1978, at Huntsville Hospital. She was adopted in South Alabama. She has green eyes, and at 10 months old, she had red hair. McDaniel said she also had a widow’s peak and a scar on her chin from stitches after falling off a step.
Nayman said if Kami doesn’t want to be found, then she will accept it. She also said if Kami doesn’t know she was adopted, the last thing she wants to do is upset her life. She just wants to exhaust every effort to let Kami know that they love her.
